query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In untreated (pre‐exposure) Q235 steel, the native iron oxide film is non‐uniform and contains defects that serve as weak points for localized anodic reactions; these discontinuities allow aggressive ions to penetrate and initiate corrosion in harsh environments, whereas a more uniform, dense passive film (achieved via a controlled mild thermal pre‐oxidation) suppresses degradation by reducing ion transfer and localized dissolution, acting through improved film continuity and chemical stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its as-received, pre-exposure state with an inherently non-uniform native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled mild oxidation (thermal pre-treatment) to foster the formation of a uniform, adherent passive oxide film on the steel surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to harsh corrosive environments at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (e.g., immersion in a moderately concentrated saline solution or simulated aggressive geothermal fluids), where both the temperature and chemical aggressiveness challenge the integrity of the oxide film.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuity, density, and chemical stability of the surface iron oxide/passive film.
generation.mechanism: In the pre-exposure state, defects and discontinuities in the native oxide facilitate localized breakdown and lapses in passivation, leading to accelerated anodic dissolution and pitting, whereas the uniform passive film retards ion migration and local corrosion reactions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Q235 steel samples that receive the mild oxidation pre-treatment should exhibit lower corrosion current densities, more noble corrosion potentials, reduced pitting occurrence, and lower weight loss compared to untreated samples when exposed to the same harsh conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel with its naturally forming, but non-uniform and defect-rich, native oxide layer.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under corrosive conditions where the passive film is critical to performance (such as in chloride-rich solutions at moderate to elevated temperatures) but may not apply at extremely high temperatures or in environments where the oxide film is inherently unstable regardless of pre-treatment.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal parameters (temperature, time, atmosphere) for the mild oxidation treatment remain to be defined, and variations in ambient contaminants or alloy microstructure might also affect film quality and the degree of corrosion suppression.

falsification_experiment.design: Take two sets of Q235 steel samples: one set remains untreated (with its native oxide) and the other is subjected to a controlled mild oxidation pre-treatment designed to form a continuous passive film. Expose both sets to a harsh corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) at room temperature and at an elevated temperature. Monitor the corrosion behavior over time using electrochemical techniques and surface morphology analysis.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization to obtain corrosion current density (icorr) and corrosion potential (Ecorr)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess charge transfer resistance
Surface analysis (SEM/optical microscopy) to quantify pitting density and oxide film continuity
Weight loss measurements over defined exposure times
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated Q235 samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance (i.e., similar or higher corrosion rates, icorr, or pitting density compared to untreated samples) under the same conditions, then the hypothesis that a uniform passive oxide layer suppresses corrosion degradation in harsh environments is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The low strength caused by the single FCC structure of the CrMnFeCoNi high entropy alloy (HEA) limits its application in the field of coating. Here, we prepared high-entropy alloy coatings of CrMnFeCoNi with different ZrC contents on Q235 steel by a plasma transferred arc process. The effects of ZrC on the microstructure and properties of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating were investigated by optical microscopy, scanning electron microscope, and X-ray diffraction and by employing a potensiostat/galvanostat. The results showed that ZrC mainly existed in the coatings as a second phase, having little influence on the main crystal structure and micromorphology of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating. The hardness of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increased with the ZrC content. ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating. In a 1 mol/L NaCl solution with 4 wt% ZrC, the annual corrosion rate was only 5.997% of that of the HEA coating. Nevertheless, the improvement in the wear resistance of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy coatings was not apparent with the addition of ZrC.
